newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ING mulls European buys, alliances.
newsitem.headline: ING mulls European buys, alliances.

text.p: Financial services group ING Groep NV (ING) is considering acquisitions or alliances in Europe as part of an increased emphasis on its home continent, executive board chairman Aad Jacobs said on Wednesday.
He said this represented a slight change of the Dutch group's previous view that it did not need to be a large player in the major European countries such as Germany and France.

Jacobs told a Dutch Foreign Press Association luncheon that it was more important to be a pan-European player in banking than in insurance and indicated that cross-shareholdings and alliances were more likely than acquisitions.
Jacobs said ING was convinced that the single European currency, the euro, would be introduced according to plan in 1999 with the Netherlands among the first participants.

ING holds 17 percent cent of the Dutch guilder market and, as its share of the euro market would be barely one percent if it did not expand, ING's strategy in the next few years would be to place more emphasis on Europe.

"If necessary, we will opt for acquisitions or alliances to extend our presence in Europe, but we are also going to develop a number of strategic initiatives based on our current know-how and strength," Jacobs told the luncheon.
ING would focus on gaining significant positions in specific segments, such as direct marketing, employee benefits, corporate finance, treasury, clearing and asset management.
He said ING was "rich enough" to make acquisitions in Europe although it did not have a specific target in mind, adding that French and German companies were in the same position.
In insurance, there was little synergy between life operations in different countries.
"But in the banking world if you want to follow your clients, its important that you have a stake in all these European countries," Jacobs said.
ING has little representation in Germany and France in banking or insurance, preferring until now to expand out of its Dutch home market into eastern European countries such as Poland and Hungary.
He said the few European banks for sale were expensive or of poor quality, adding that it was much too early to talk of a major acquisition.
"What we can do, if there's interest, is to make alliances and (take) cross-shareholdings," he said, declining to say when this could occur.
